newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: GOVERNMENT WELCOMES TOYOTA EXPANSION
Federal Industry minister John Moore says Toyota's investment expansion in Australia is an early confirmation of the success of the Government's industry strategy.
Toyota says it will invest up to $1-billion dollars over the next eight years, with $80-million to be spent on producing its first large car, to roll off the Victorian assembly line in the year 2000.
Mr Moore says the Government's recent decision to freeze car tariffs was designed to secure investment in the lead up to trade liberalisation in 2010.
The Minister says Japan's leading car manufacturers have a very positive view of Australia and the Government's strategy of providing stability for the industry to encourage further investment here.
TELSTRA BILLING PROBED
An investigation has been launched into Telstra's billing arrangements with the range of new telecommunication service providers now competing against it.
The new companies, which buy bulk access to Telstra's phone network and then re-sell the services, have claimed Telstra's approach to billing is unfair and unduly harsh.

Communications Minister Richard Alston said the investigation into the billing relationship was designed to ensure there were no impediments to open competition in the newly de-regulated telecommunications market.
Senator Alston said the consultants conducting the inquiry would talk to the new service providers to assess the impact any billing problems have on their customers.
Telstra says it's happy with the new investigation into its billing arrangements.
Telstra says it believes the investigation will identify any deficiencies in the billing arrangements, and help instill confidence in the marketplace.
COMMISSIONER GIVEN NAMES OF SUSPECTED PAEDOPHILES
A Queensland Labor MP today handed the names of suspected paedophiles to the Children's Commissioner.
Member for Whitsunday Lorraine Bird says she has also provided dates of suspected illegal activities to the Commissioner, although admits she does not have any hard evidence.
Mrs Bird also handed over boxes of hearsay evidence to the Parliamentary Criminal Justice Committee in the early 1990s.
Meanwhile, Queensland Opposition leader Peter Beattie is calling for a Royal Commission to investigate the paedophile allegations.

"This is a matter of such seriousness to the fabric of our society it should be properly and fully investigated, and a Royal Commission is clearly one of the ways that should be done," Mr Beattie said.
"It shouldn't have any blurring of people's roles, we should have it all out in the open," he said.
In another development, Mackay ABC journalist Col Wilson has been asked to provide material to the Children's Commissioner about the paedophile activities of Theo Watts Brown.
Watts Brown was charged with indecently dealing with a boy in Sydney, but died in a car accident in 1993 before the case was heard in court.
Col Wilson has been conducting research for a book on Watts Brown, and obtained diary notes and phone records from his home in the Whitsundays.
He has travelled from Mackay to hand the material to the Children's Commissioner today.
A report on paedophilia in Queensland is due to be tabled in parliament tomorrow.
KNUCKLES RAPPED FOR PACIFIC DOCUMENT LEAK
Disciplinary action has been taken against four Federal Treasury officials over the publication last month of a confidential briefing paper on South Pacific political figures.
The document, which described some South Pacific leaders as corrupt and incompetent, was left on an open table at a conference of regional leaders in Cairns.
Publication of the briefing paper's contents sparked outrage in the region, threatening Australia's relations with a number of island nations.
An internal inquiry has resulted in a senior Treasury official being stripped of a year's performance pay, and three other officers receiving disciplinary counselling.
The inquiry says leaving the documents unattended at the Cairns conference was a serious breach of security, and was the result of an unfortunate chain of circumstances.
DEAD TREES MAY BE REPLACED IN MURRAY RIVER
Snags, or dead trees, removed from the Murray River over the past century could be replaced, in a move aimed at boosting native fish numbers.
The snags provide a natural habitat and their loss has endangered the Murray Cod, Trout Cod and Yellow Belly.
Scientists have gathered information on the species' preferred habitat, by tracing the fish through radio tracking.
John Koehn from the Marine and Freshwater Resources Institute, says putting dead trees back into the water will help reverse the decline.
"The big problem will be the source of timber," Mr Koehn said.
He said it may be that timber could be taken from the excess of forestry operations such as Redgum cutting, or from farm paddocks, and used in the river.
Mr Koehn said placing the timber in the river would be a logistical problem that would have to be worked on.
TRAIN TURNS BACK FROM BREAKING COAL STRIKE
A train sent in to try to break the 14 week Curragh Coal strike in central Queensland has turned back.
The train waited at the picket line for two hours while the crew consulted with their union, but it eventually reversed away from the mine, accompanied by applause from the striking workers.
Curragh mine owners Arco have also announced a temporary closure of the nearby Gordonstone mine, with all workers to be retrenched and selected staff to be re-employed under new conditions.

Miners Union Federal President John Maitland warned Arco and other mining companies against taking on the union movement. Mr Maitland said it had been suggested there was a link between a number of companies in Queensland who were anxious to "take on" the trade union movement.
"All I can say is that they do that at their own folly," he said.

"It's already been proved that Australian workers will not stand for foreign companies discriminating against their workforce. And I think that the public in general will not accept this sort of attack on the rights of trade unionists."
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
